Survey: Police struggle for public trust as Army tops approval ratings
description:
The Bangladesh Army enjoys by far the strongest public approval among major national institutions, while police are the only institution surveyed where disapproval outweighs approval, according to the latest International Republican Institute (IRI) survey.

The findings reveal a sharp contrast in how Bangladeshis perceive different state and social institutions, with the Army receiving an approval rating of 78%.

The High Court and local government institutions, upazila parishads and city corporations, follow with approval ratings of around 61% each.

The media receives about 59% approval, while religious leaders stand at around 58%.

Public assessments become less positive further down the institutional rankings.

The student movement receives an approval rating of about 56%, while the Election Commission stands at roughly 53%.

Political parties collectively fare worse, receiving around 51% approval.

Police sit at the bottom of the list.

Only 45% approve of the job police are doing, while 52% disapprove, making police the only institution covered by the question with a negative net approval rating.

The findings are significant as Bangladesh continues to debate institutional reform and public confidence in state agencies following the political upheaval of 2024 and the February 2026 national election.

IRI asked respondents whether they strongly or somewhat approved or disapproved of the performance of nine institutions and groups: the Army, High Court, local government bodies, media, religious leaders, student movement, Election Commission, political parties and police.

The results suggest that public confidence varies substantially across institutions, with security institutions themselves receiving sharply different assessments.

The nationwide survey was conducted among 5,000 voting-age adults between May 16 and June 24, with a margin of error of ±1.7 percentage points.

title: IRI survey: Bangladesh almost evenly split over country’s direction
description:
Bangladeshis are almost evenly divided over whether the country is moving in the right direction, with public optimism declining since late last year, according to the latest International Republican Institute (IRI) survey.

The nationwide poll found that 46% of respondents believe Bangladesh is heading in the right direction, while 44% think it is moving in the wrong direction. Another 9% did not know or declined to answer.

The narrow two-point gap marks a significant shift from October 2025, when 53% believed the country was heading in the right direction and 42% said the opposite.

The findings suggest that the optimism recorded last year has weakened as Bangladesh navigates its post-election political and economic transition.

The mood also varies considerably across the country.

Rangpur emerged as the most optimistic division, with 59% saying Bangladesh was heading in the right direction. Barisal followed at 52% and Chittagong at 51%.

At the other end, only 29% of respondents in Sylhet said the country was moving in the right direction, while 59% said it was heading the wrong way.

Dhaka was also more pessimistic than optimistic, with 42% saying right direction against 48% saying wrong direction.

Among those who said Bangladesh was heading in the wrong direction, the most frequently cited reason was rising commodity prices, mentioned by 18%.

Another 17% pointed to deterioration in law and order and the judicial situation, while 10% cited increasing corruption.

Gas shortages, lack of employment opportunities and low agricultural prices were among the other concerns.

The findings show that the public verdict on the country’s overall trajectory remains finely balanced despite comparatively positive assessments of democracy recorded elsewhere in the same survey.

IRI surveyed 5,000 adults across all 64 districts between May 16 and June 24.

title: Govt approves Tk68.50 crore budget for workers' welfare in current fiscal
description:
The Ministry of Labour and Employment on Sunday approved a Tk68.50 crore budget for the Bangladesh Labour Welfare Foundation for FY27, alongside financial grants worth Tk12.98 crore for 2,199 workers and their families from both formal and informal sectors.

The decisions were taken at the 34th board meeting of the Foundation, held at the ministry's conference room on Sunday afternoon, with Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury presiding.

Speaking at the meeting, the minister said ensuring the welfare of the working class, standing by them in times of crisis, and strengthening the social safety net remain among the government's top priorities.

He said workers from both the formal and informal sectors continue to labour tirelessly, day and night, to keep the national economy moving and production systems running, adding that the country's development journey is being accelerated on the strength of their sweat and unrelenting effort.

The minister said the goal is to ensure that no working person feels alone in times of distress, noting that the ministry and the Foundation remain committed to protecting the rights and life security of workers at all times.

He expressed confidence that a balanced, work-friendly and exploitation-free labour policy and environment could be built through the coordinated efforts of government officials, employers and workers' organizations.

Labour and Employment Secretary Md Abdur Rahman Tarafder, Bangladesh Sramik Kalyan Foundation Director General Mohammad Kuddus Ali Sarker, Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal President Anwar Hossain, representatives from various ministries, and representatives from both workers' and employers' sides were present at the meeting.

title: IRI survey: BNP gains public favour as Jamaat loses ground
description:
Public attitudes towards Bangladesh’s major political parties have shifted since last year, with the BNP gaining favour while Jamaat-e-Islami has lost ground, according to the latest nationwide survey by the International Republican Institute (IRI).

The June 2026 survey shows that 57% of respondents hold a favourable view of the BNP, up from 51% in October 2025.

The increase gives the party the highest favourability among the major political forces measured in the survey.

Jamaat-e-Islami, meanwhile, moved in the opposite direction. Its favourability fell to 48%, down from 53% in October last year.

The findings point to a changing political landscape following the February 2026 national parliamentary election.

The National Citizen Party (NCP), which emerged from the political realignment following the July 2024 uprising, remains further behind the two established parties.

Its favourability stands at around 37%, little changed from the previous survey.

The Awami League continues to face the most difficult public perception among the major parties surveyed.

Only around 22% of respondents expressed favourable views of the party, while roughly 72% viewed it unfavourably.

IRI asked respondents whether they strongly or somewhat liked or disliked nine political parties, including the BNP, Jamaat, NCP, Islami Andolan Bangladesh, Awami League and Jatiya Party.

The latest findings are particularly significant because they capture public attitudes several months after the February election, providing an early indication of how the country’s political forces are being perceived in the post-election environment.

The survey was conducted between May 16 and June 24 among 5,000 adults across all 64 districts. IRI said the nationally representative survey has a margin of error of ±1.7 percentage points.

title: Dhaka asks Delhi to expedite Hasina extradition, return Hadi killers
description:
The extradition of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the return of Osman Hadi murder accused were among the key issues discussed between Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi on Monday.

“Bangladesh hopes that India will expedite the process of extraditing Sheikh Hasina,” said a press release issued by the PM’s Press Wing after the meeting.

At the same time, the request to India to return to Bangladesh the killers involved in the murder of Shaheed Osman Hadi has been reiterated.

Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi paid the courtesy call on the prime minister at his office at the Secretariat around 11:00 am.

Dinesh Trivedi formally assumed office after presenting his credentials to former president Mohammed Shahabuddin on 25 June.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman welcomed Trivedi at the beginning of the meeting.

The Indian high commissioner briefed the prime minister on his experience during his first two months in Dhaka, said Shahadat Shadhin, the prime minister’s deputy press secretary.

The meeting covered a range of important bilateral issues between Bangladesh and India.

The prime minister stressed the need to create a suitable environment to further strengthen bilateral relations between the two countries.

This was Trivedi’s first meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman and the Prime Minister’s Foreign Affairs Adviser Humayun Kabir were present during the meeting.

India appointed Trivedi, a former Indian railway minister and health minister and a veteran politician from West Bengal, as its 16th High Commissioner to Bangladesh in April replacing Pranay Kumar Verma.

Indian high commissioner meets Tarique Rahman

Dinesh Trivedi formally assumed office after presenting his credentials to former president Mohammed Shahabuddin on 25 June.

Trivedi has already held meetings with Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman and State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed as part of his diplomatic engagements in Dhaka.

PM: Govt committed to building democratic, welfare-oriented state
description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has said the government is working to build Bangladesh as a democratic and welfare-oriented state, with efforts underway to rebuild sectors devastated over the past one and a half decades.

“For more than a decade and a half, the fascist government destroyed the country’s education, healthcare, economy and other sectors. Now it is time to rebuild them,” he said. “We are continuing our efforts towards that goal. We believe the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) will play an indispensable role in the country’s rebuilding journey.”

The prime minister made the remarks on Monday afternoon while inaugurating three SDG villages under the SDG Village Pilot Programme at the China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka.

Joining the event virtually, he formally inaugurated the three villages, Mitingachhari in Kaptai, Rangamati; Pankhali in Dacope, Khulna; and Nafanagar in Bochaganj, Dinajpur.

Tarique Rahman said no single ministry or department can achieve the SDG targets alone, stressing the need for cooperation from all relevant stakeholders.

He said the government’s people-oriented policies are aligned with the SDG principle of “leaving no one behind.” The government’s policy is “Bangladesh for All,” aimed at safeguarding the interests of people from all walks of life.

The prime minister said Bangladesh had demonstrated significant success in implementing the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and is similarly taking appropriate measures to effectively implement the SDGs.

Local Government Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir and Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury also attended the event.

title: Foreign minister: Govt yet to decide on PMs’ BRICS Summit attendance
description:
Foreign Minister Dr Khalilur Rahman on Monday said the government has not yet decided whether Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will attend the outreach session of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi next month, while urging the media to distinguish between two separate invitations extended by India.

“One is an invitation from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for a bilateral visit, while the other is an invitation for the BIMSTEC chair to attend the BRICS Summit,” Khalilur told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

“First of all, I am not an astrologer. So, I cannot predict on which exact day it will happen,” he said when asked about the prime minister’s possible visit.

He also clarified that the invitation to attend the BRICS outreach session was not addressed to Tarique Rahman personally, but to Bangladesh in his capacity as chair of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC).

Khalilur was briefing reporters after Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat.

On August 4, India confirmed that it had invited Tarique to attend the BRICS Summit as the current BIMSTEC chair, while a separate invitation for a bilateral visit to India has been in place since February.

“You would be aware that a formal invitation to Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit India was extended when he assumed office in February 2026,” Indian Ministry of External Affairs Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a recent media briefing in New Delhi.

“India has separately extended an invitation to the Bangladesh Prime Minister in his capacity as the current Chair of BIMSTEC to attend the outreach session of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi,” he said.

Jaiswal said the invitation was extended in line with the standard practice followed by BRICS for its outreach sessions, with other heads of regional groupings invited in a similar manner.

India will host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, with discussions expected to focus on global cooperation, trade and sustainable development.

During Monday’s meeting, High Commissioner Trivedi conveyed greetings from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and expressed India’s intention to work with the government and people of Bangladesh in a positive, constructive and forward-looking manner.

The two sides exchanged views on matters of mutual interest and discussed ways to further strengthen bilateral relations through a people-centric approach.

Trivedi also paid a courtesy call on Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, with discussions focusing on bilateral relations and areas of common interest, including security cooperation.

The high commissioner conveyed India’s willingness to strengthen people-centric cooperation in all areas based on mutual interest, mutual benefit and mutual sensitivities.

BIMSTEC comprises seven countries — Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand.

Bangladesh assumed the chairmanship of BIMSTEC in April 2025 for a two-year term, with a commitment to advancing regional cooperation and development.

title: No interchange fee for Bangla QR transactions from October 1
description:
To boost digital transactions nationwide, Bangladesh Bank has reset the interchange reimbursement fee (IRF) to zero for all Bangla QR code-based transactions, effective October 1.

Consequently, card or account issuers will no longer receive any fee or service charge from acquiring institutions for Bangla QR transactions.

The Payment Systems Department-2 of Bangladesh Bank issued a circular letter on Monday instructing all scheduled banks, Mobile Financial Service (MFS) providers, Payment Service Providers (PSPs), and Payment System Operators (PSOs) to implement the directive.

According to the central bank, this adjustment amends previous instructions issued in Payment Systems Department Circular No. 02/2025 on February 6, 2025.

Additionally, directives under Circular Letter No. 05 issued on July 1 this year will be repealed starting October 1, while all other existing guidelines remain unchanged.

Bangladesh Bank previously made Bangla QR usage mandatory for merchants starting July 1.

As Bangla QR enables merchants to accept payments from multiple banks and MFS providers through a single unified QR code, it has become a central component of Bangladesh's cashless transaction strategy.

Financial industry experts expect that eliminating inter-institutional transaction costs will significantly lower merchant expenses and accelerate consumer adoption of QR-based digital payments across the country.

title: Banks warned on source tax deduction from deposit interest
description:
Bangladesh Bank has cautioned all scheduled banks to accurately deduct tax deducted at source (TDS) from interest and profit paid on deposits and deposit them into the government treasury within prescribed deadlines.

The Banking Regulation and Policy Department-1 of Bangladesh Bank issued a circular letter on Monday, instructing the managing directors and chief executive officers of all operational banks to strictly comply with source tax regulations under the Income Tax Act, 2023.

The central bank noted recent irregularities where banks either failed to deduct TDS at the appropriate rate or delayed transferring the collected tax into the government exchequer.

Such discrepancies have created complexities during tax audits and adjustments, while also depriving the government of legitimate tax revenue.

Under Section 102 of the Income Tax Act, 2023, banks must deduct TDS on interest or profits paid across all savings, fixed, term, or other deposit accounts based on the account holder's category.

Under Section 142 of the same Act, if an account holder fails to provide Proof of Submission of Return (PSR), the bank must deduct or collect TDS at a rate 50% higher than the standard rate.

In line with Rule 8 of the Income Tax Rules, 2023, tax collected between July and May must be deposited into the government treasury within two weeks following the end of the collection month.

For tax collected in the first 20 days of June, the transfer must occur within seven days; for any tax deducted during the rest of June, it must be deposited the very next day.

Bangladesh Bank explicitly prohibited banks from retaining collected source taxes in general ledgers or temporary accounts beyond these stipulated limits.

Banks were also mandated to maintain meticulous records of all TDS deductions and submit copies of returns and deposit challans to the relevant tax authorities.

The directive was issued under powers conferred by Section 45 of the Bank Company Act, 1991.

title: Foreign minister at briefing: Dhaka seeks enabling environment to advance Bangladesh–India ties
description:
Bangladesh has urged India to help create a conducive environment for advancing relations between the two neighbouring countries. The message was conveyed during Indian High Commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi’s first courtesy meeting with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday morning.

Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman disclosed the matter to journalists at a briefing at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the afternoon, following the meeting at the prime minister’s secretariat.

He said emphasis had been placed on creating the kind of “enabling environment” necessary to take bilateral relations forward.

The foreign minister said Bangladesh had also urged New Delhi to expedite the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been sentenced to death for crimes against humanity, and is currently in India.

Dhaka also requested the extradition of those suspected of murdering Inqilab Moncho convenor Shaheed Sharif Osman Bin Hadi, he added.

Referring to reports that Hadi’s suspected killers had been apprehended in India, Khalilur Rahman said, “We have provided them with all the documents they requested. This is an extremely sensitive issue for us [the Hadi case]. We have asked them to extradite the killers to us as soon as possible.”

Asked whether the issues of border killings and push-ins had been discussed during the meeting, the foreign minister said they had, albeit briefly.

“These are not matters for discussion at the prime ministerial level,” he said, adding that the issues had been discussed during his meeting with the Indian high commissioner yesterday, Sunday.

Asked whether Bangladesh’s earlier expression of displeasure to India over the events of 5 August had come up in Monday’s discussion, Khalilur Rahman said, “We have clearly stated our position regarding 5 August, and the Indian authorities have taken it seriously. They told me this yesterday, and they told the prime minister the same thing today.”

There will be issues, and they will be resolved: Dinesh Trivedi

Asked whether India had expressed regret over allowing Sheikh Hasina to address a press conference in New Delhi on 5 August, the second anniversary of the July uprising, the foreign minister said the matter should not be framed simply in terms of an apology.

“You have to understand clearly what happened,” he said. “A state has three branches—the executive, the legislature and the judiciary. Convicted Hasina belongs to the jurisdiction of the judiciary. A court in Bangladesh tried her and sentenced her. What happens in the case of a convicted person? They are taken into custody, and if they have anything to say in their defence, they say it before the court.”

Elaborating on the matter, Khalilur Rahman said, “What Hasina did on 5 August was to spread hatred against Bangladesh’s judiciary—one of the three branches of the state—and the Indian government allowed her to do so.”

He added, “As I said yesterday, we want every country to respect the entire constitutional structure of our state. We hope the Indian government will understand and appreciate this, and I believe they have understood the matter. We hope they will not do anything further that undermines any branch of our state. Based on my discussions with them, I am somewhat reassured, and I hope there will be no recurrence of such an incident.”

Dhaka asks Delhi to expedite Hasina extradition, return Hadi killers

Asked whether the Bangladesh government had accepted an invitation for Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to visit New Delhi after India extended invitations to him on two occasions, the foreign minister said, “First of all, I am not a fortune-teller. Secondly, the prime minister was not invited to BRICS. He was invited as the chair of BIMSTEC. You should try to understand that distinction.”

He further said that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had previously sent a letter to Bangladesh’s prime minister, which was handed over on the day the new government was formed. “There is an invitation,” he said.

Asked in a follow-up question whether the invitation to visit Delhi had been discussed when the Indian high commissioner met the prime minister on Monday, Khalilur Rahman said, “We have not yet taken any decision on this.”

title: Record July heat in regions home to 900m people
description:
Regions home to around 900 million people experienced their hottest July on record in 2026, including in the Sahel, Central America, France and Spain, according to AFP analysis of Copernicus data.

Some 33 countries recorded their hottest July since records began, according to a detailed analysis of billions of data points from Copernicus’s ERA5 climate model.

Some countries with well-resourced national weather agencies, including France and Spain, independently confirmed record-breaking conditions through analyses by Meteo-France and Spain’s Aemet meteorological service.

However, many lower-income countries do not publish detailed climate data.

AFP therefore complemented the global picture by independently analyzing data from the European Copernicus program.

The dataset combines observations from satellites operated by multiple countries, weather stations on land, at sea and in the air, together with climate modelling. It provides hourly global coverage dating back to 1970.

Nearly 400 million of the roughly 900 million people residing in affected areas live in Africa, primarily within the Sahel region.

Ten countries in the semi-arid belt across western and northern Africa broke their monthly heat records for July, including Mauritania, Niger and Burkina Faso.

In eastern Africa, Sudan, Kenya and Ethiopia also broke records.

Temperature variations and anomalies in countries close to the equator are typically smaller than in temperate climates.

Yet countries such as Chad and Sudan recorded July temperatures more than 2°C above the 1981-2010 average.

Episodes of extreme heat have become almost 10 times more likely since 2015, scientists from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) network warned in January, attributing the rise to human-driven climate change.

Sahel countries are among the most vulnerable to rising temperatures, while many are already grappling with armed conflict, food insecurity and widespread poverty.

The naturally-occurring El Nino climate pattern, which began in June and is expected to peak later this year, has already amplified unprecedented temperatures across Central America and northern South America.

From Mexico to northern Brazil, stretching from the Pacific coast to the Guiana Highlands, approximately 110 million people experienced their hottest July on record.

El Salvador, Nicaragua and Honduras, located in the so-called “Dry Corridor,” all set monthly temperature records in both June and July, heightening concerns over famine.

The United Nations World Food Program (WFP) said last week that Central America is expected to be the region hardest hit in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity.

Including the Caribbean, the agency estimates that an additional 16 million people could face food insecurity by the end of 2027.

Nearly 120 million Europeans live in regions where July 2026 was the hottest ever recorded.

The records were concentrated in southern Britain, western France, and northern and eastern Spain.

In France, average temperatures were 3.8°C above the 1991-2020 normal -- a reference period already significantly warmer than the pre-industrial climate of 1850-1900.

France and Spain also registered record levels of drought, which fueled devastating wildfires.

A megafire burned nearly 42,000 hectares and forced the evacuation of more than 220,000 people in France’s Gironde department in late July.

At the same time, Spain’s largest wildfire in recent history scorched almost 44,000 hectares in Avila province, near Madrid.

Other smaller and more scattered regions, home to a combined population of over 250 million, also experienced unprecedented July heat, including China’s Sichuan province, US states Wyoming and Colorado and the Indonesian islands of Sumatra and Borneo.

Nearly 7 lakh fail as SSC pass rate hits 19-year low
description:
Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and equivalent examinations have delivered one of the starkest warnings yet about the state of secondary education, with nearly four in every 10 candidates failing this year as the national pass rate plunged to 62.25%, its lowest level since 2007.

The decline is not confined to the headline pass rate.

GPA-5 achievements have fallen sharply, the number of institutions where every candidate failed has more than doubled, boys are trailing girls by a wide margin, and humanities students have emerged as particularly vulnerable.

The results have brought longstanding weaknesses in English and mathematics, teacher shortages, classroom learning and curriculum implementation back into focus, raising a larger question over whether years of relatively high pass rates had masked deeper learning deficiencies.

Of the 1,829,485 candidates who appeared in the SSC and equivalent examinations this year, 1,138,897 passed and 690,608 failed.

The pass rate fell 6.20 percentage points from 68.45% in 2025.

The number of GPA-5 achievers also dropped by 22,356, from 139,032 last year to 116,676 this year.

The last time the national pass rate was lower was in 2007, when 58.36% of candidates passed.

From 93% to 62% in five years

The scale of the decline becomes more striking against Bangladesh’s recent examination history.

After standing at 72.18% in 2008, the pass rate crossed 80% in 2011 and remained above that level for seven consecutive years. It peaked at 91.34% in 2014.

The Covid-affected examination of 2021, conducted with fewer subjects and a shortened syllabus, produced an exceptional 93.58% pass rate.

Since then, the trajectory has largely been downward, 87.44% in 2022 and 80.39% in 2023, before a temporary rise to 83.04% in 2024.

With full marks and the full syllabus returning, the rate plunged to 68.45% in 2025 and has now fallen further to 62.25%.

The two consecutive years of steep decline have strengthened concerns that the problem goes beyond tougher examinations or stricter evaluation.

English and mathematics have emerged as major pressure points, particularly for humanities students.

Prof Syed Akhtaruzzaman, chairman of the Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee and Dhaka Education Board, said humanities students performed particularly poorly in the two subjects, while science students did relatively better.

The results show the scale of the problem.

Among male humanities candidates under the nine general education boards, only 41.14% passed.

The rate among female humanities candidates was 54.38%.

The recurring weakness in English and mathematics raises questions over why learning gaps in two fundamental subjects are not being identified and addressed before students reach the SSC examination.

Teacher shortages could be another part of the problem.

Parents have complained that some schools are operating with substantially fewer teachers than required, leaving students increasingly dependent on private tuition, coaching or their own resources.

Educationist Dr Siddiqur Rahman Khan pointed to broader weaknesses in curriculum implementation, teacher training, remuneration and benefits, questioning how such large numbers could fail after completing school-level selection examinations and receiving additional preparation time.

Perhaps the strongest institutional warning comes from schools where not a single candidate passed.

Across the nine general education boards, 312 institutions recorded a zero pass rate, up from 134 last year, an increase of nearly 133%.

At the other end, the number of institutions achieving a 100% pass rate fell from 984 to 669.

The figures raise questions that go well beyond individual student performance.

When every candidate from an institution fails, educationists say issues such as teacher availability, attendance, school management, academic supervision and students’ socio-economic circumstances require scrutiny.

Where students studied also appears to have made a considerable difference.

Dhaka topped the nine general boards with a 71.63% pass rate, while Mymensingh finished at the bottom with 57.39%.

Jessore recorded 66.27%, Comilla 65.42%, Rajshahi 63.67%, Barisal 60.35%, Chittagong 59.48%, Sylhet 58.33% and Dinajpur 58.05%.

The Madrasa Education Board recorded a pass rate of 55.49%, while the Technical Education Board stood at 58.20%.

The disparities add another dimension to the challenge: whether students across Bangladesh have comparable access to teachers, learning environments and academic support.

Educationists attributed the sharp fall in SSC results to a combination of unresolved Covid-era learning losses, instability in educational institutions following the 2024 movement, teacher shortages, curriculum changes and stricter evaluation.

Educationist Rasheda K Chowdhury said: “It would not be right to call it a disaster, because this may be the real picture. We could not recover from the setback caused by Covid.”

She also pointed to prolonged instability and a shortage of skilled, subject-based teachers, particularly outside major cities.

Education researcher KM Enamul Haque said stricter evaluation may have contributed to the decline, but identified pandemic-era learning loss as a deeper problem.

Enamul said: “The students sitting for the examination now entered Class VI, or the secondary level, in 2020. They entered secondary education with a major learning deficit from primary school and have carried that gap with them. This year’s results are strong evidence of that.”

Md Rahmat Ullah, former principal of Kishloy Girls’ School and College, also cited stricter evaluation, curriculum changes and prolonged disruption.

Rahmat said: “Students also went through a prolonged period of unrest when they could not concentrate properly on their studies.”

Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, however, rejected the characterisation of the results as a disaster.

He described the result as not bad but “beautiful”, defending evaluation based on what students actually wrote in their answer scripts.

Students dissatisfied with their results, he said, have the opportunity to seek re-evaluation.

But the scale and breadth of this year’s decline leave questions that re-evaluation alone cannot answer.

The 690,608 failures, 312 zero-pass institutions, widening gender disparity and persistent weakness in fundamental subjects provide policymakers with multiple indicators requiring deeper investigation.

Restoring an 80% or 90% pass rate, educationists caution, should not itself become the objective. Easier examinations or more generous marking could improve the statistics without improving learning.

Instead, the results provide an opportunity to examine what students actually know, where they begin falling behind, whether schools have enough qualified teachers and why weaknesses in fundamental subjects remain unresolved until the end of secondary education.

The most consequential number in this year’s SSC results may therefore not be 62.25%.

It is the 690,608 students who reached the end of secondary education but could not cross its principal public examination, a figure that turns a poor examination result into a warning for the education system itself.

title: Coal dominates Bangladesh’s top imports, clinker at second position
description:
Around 5,700 categories of goods are imported into Bangladesh each year. The list includes industrial raw materials, fuel, consumer goods and various materials used in development projects.

However, imports of only a handful of these thousands of products account for a huge volume. Some products are imported in quantities exceeding tens of millions of tonnes a year.

An analysis of data from the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and its field offices shows that a total of 158.6 million tonnes of goods were imported through the country’s 46 customs stations in the recently concluded 2025–26 financial year.

The top 10 products accounted for 99.8 million tonnes. In other words, nearly 63kg of every 100kg of imported goods came from these 10 products.

Industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction dominate the top 10. Among food grains, only wheat made the list.

LNG: 13-year import deal secured with one US firm

Clinker loses top spot after 25 years

According to NBR data, clinker—the main raw material used to make cement—was the country’s largest imported product by volume for 25 consecutive years, from the 2000–01 to 2024–25 financial year. That long-standing dominance has now come to an end.

Coal displaced clinker to become the country’s largest imported product in the 2025–26 financial year. Bangladesh imported 20.7 million tonnes of coal during the year.

Several raw materials, including slag, limestone and fly ash, are used alongside clinker in cement production. All four feature among the top 10 imported products.

The rise in coal imports is not unexpected. Demand for coal has increased rapidly for power generation since coal-fired power plants began operating in the country. Six coal-fired power plants accounted for around 75 per cent of total coal imports last financial year.

As a result, coal, once used mainly as fuel and a raw material in industrial factories, has now become the country’s largest imported product by volume.

Clinker second, slag fourth

Clinker, a raw material used in cement production, has dropped to second place after losing its long-held position at the top. The country imported 19.2 million tonnes of clinker in the last financial year.

Several raw materials, including slag, limestone and fly ash, are used alongside clinker in cement production. All four feature among the top 10 imported products. After clinker, another cement raw material, slag, ranks fourth. The country imported 8.3 million tonnes of slag in the last financial year.

Limestone, which ranks sixth, accounted for nearly 6 million tonnes of imports. And, Fly ash, or ash, ranks 10th, with imports of around 5 million tonnes.

Wheat is the only consumer product among the top 10 imported goods. By volume, it ranks fifth. Bangladesh imported 7.434 million tonnes of wheat in the last financial year.

In total, nearly 38.5 million tonnes of the four types of cement raw materials were imported. In other words, cement industry raw materials account for a substantial share of the total volume of the top 10 imported products.

Crushed stone ranks third

Crushed stone ranks third by import volume. Bangladesh imported 16.8 million tonnes of crushed stone in the last financial year. The stone is used in the construction of roads, buildings and various other infrastructure projects.

Alongside crushed stone, large quantities of boulder stone are also imported. The country imported 5.5 million tonnes of boulder stone in 2025-26 financial year, placing it eighth by volume. Boulder stone is used in river management and various development projects.

Wheat the only consumer product in top 10

Wheat is the only consumer product among the top 10 imported goods. By volume, it ranks fifth. Bangladesh imported 7.434 million tonnes of wheat in the last financial year.

Approximately 15 per cent of the country’s demand for wheat is met by domestic production. The remaining 85 per cent or so is met through imports. As a result, wheat is the country’s largest imported food grain by volume.

Amirul Haque, president, Chattogram ChamberMost of the products imported in the largest volumes are industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction. Five of them are raw materials for the cement and steel sectors. Demand for these products will increase as economic activity and investment grow.

Scrap, the raw material for rebar, ranks seventh

Scrap metal, or old iron and iron pieces, the main raw material used to make rebar, ranks seventh. Bangladesh imported around 5.7 million tonnes of scrap in the last financial year. The country’s steel mills melt the scrap to produce billets, which are then used to manufacture rebar and other steel products.

LNG ranks ninth

Liquefied natural gas (LNG), imported to meet fuel demand, ranks ninth. The country imported around 5.1 million tonnes of LNG in the last financial year.

Bangladesh has been importing LNG for several years to make up for shortages in domestic gas supplies. Imported LNG is converted back into gas and supplied to the national grid.

Overall, the top 10 imported products are dominated by fuels such as coal and LNG, raw materials for the cement and steel industries, and materials used in infrastructure construction. Wheat is the only food product on the list.

Bangladesh pledges to import US agricultural goods worth $3.5 billion: US envoy

This means that, by volume, a large share of Bangladesh’s imports is not directly intended for consumption but is used for power generation, industrial production and infrastructure development.

Asked for his views, Amirul Haque, an entrepreneur in the cement and consumer goods sectors and president of the Chattogram Chamber, told Prothom Alo, “Most of the products imported in the largest volumes are industrial raw materials, fuel and materials used in infrastructure construction.”

“Five of them are raw materials for the cement and steel sectors. Demand for these products will also increase as economic activity and investment grow,” he added.

Ukraine says Russia fired N Korean missiles in deadly attack
description:
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least nine people overnight and wounded dozens, Kyiv said Tuesday, accusing Moscow of launching North Korean missiles in the raid.

The allegation comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned -- without providing evidence -- that Moscow was receiving more ballistic projectiles and troops from its ally Pyongyang.

Russia has turned to North Korea for support throughout its four-and-a-half-year invasion.

Earlier in the war, Pyongyang dispatched thousands of troops to help Russia fight back a Ukrainian counterattack into its western Kursk region.

And intelligence from the West, Kyiv and Seoul, has long accused North Korea of supplying weapons to Russia.

The southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia was worst hit in Russia’s latest overnight barrage, with six people killed and 19 wounded, Zelensky said.

“The city was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons, and guided aerial bombs. It was a vicious attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage specifically on civilian infrastructure,” he said.

Three more were killed by Russian drones and missiles in the neighboring Dnipropetrovsk region, the local military administration said.

In the capital Kyiv, Zelensky said an infectious diseases hospital was hit, while strikes on the frontlines cities of Kherson and Kharkiv caused power outages.

A children’s hospital in Kyiv was also hit, the health ministry said, posting photos of broken windows and debris in a courtyard.

“Children and medical staff were not harmed, as they were in a shelter at the time of the attack,” the ministry said.

Russia’s defense ministry said its forces “delivered a group strike with high-precision ground-based weapons, hitting military-industrial enterprises and transport-logistics centers in the cities of Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia.”

Zelensky has recently renewed his warnings of deepening military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang, while appealing for more Western air-defense supplies.

On Monday, he said that Russia received “additional ballistic missiles from North Korea.”

Over the weekend, he alleged “a decision has been made for 30,000 to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on the territory of Russia.”

Kyiv has not explained how it obtained the figures and did not provide a timeframe for the deployment.

But Zelensky is urging allies in the Asia-Pacific to supply air defense to Kyiv in order to counter Pyongyang’s capabilities.

Russia and North Korea signed a mutual defense pact in 2024, ahead of Pyongyang sending troops to help push Ukrainian forces out of Russia’s Kursk region.

In recent weeks, Russia has considerably stepped up strikes with ballistic missiles -- a fast and powerful weapon that is hard to intercept.

Dozens have been killed in Kyiv in the attacks.

Only the most advanced air defense, such as the US-made Patriot system, is capable of intercepting them.

Ukraine has been reporting an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors since the US-Israeli war against Iran began in February.

Kyiv has also boosted its own long-range drone strikes against Russia, hitting oil infrastructure and e-commerce warehouses in counterattacks it says are justified and designed to crimp Moscow’s logistics and revenue sources.

The latest spiral of escalation has brought the civilian death toll in Ukraine to the highest since the war’s first months in 2022, according to the United Nations.

description:

Data compiled by Bangladesh Apparel Voice from Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) records reveals that while demand weakened across major legacy destinations like Germany, France, the UK, and Canada, the sector recorded strong month-on-month momentum—jumping 14.73% compared to June’s $3.38 billion.

title: Bank Resolution Act: Cabinet repeals controversial provision
description:
In a major policy shift for financial sector governance, the Cabinet has officially approved the draft Bank Resolution (Amendment) Act, 2026, permanently repealing the controversial Provision 18(A).

The decision closes any legal avenues for ousted controlling shareholders, former directors, and distressed business conglomerates—most notably the S Alam Group—to reclaim ownership, assets, or management control of restructured or merged banking institutions.

Chaired at the Bangladesh Secretariat on Monday (August 10), the Cabinet granted both principle and final approval for the amendment, subject to final vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.

The move eliminates the "market-based rehabilitation" loop that previously allowed former owners of non-viable banks to regain corporate control by injecting new capital or settling outstanding liabilities.

Former controlling shareholders, board members, and affiliated groups responsible for bank distress are strictly prohibited from regaining ownership or managerial control under resolution frameworks.

This eliminates the conditional mechanism introduced in the Bank Resolution Ordinance 2025 (later enacted as the Bank Resolution Act 2026) that permitted former owners to re-acquire bank shares upon fulfilling capital adequacy conditions.

Blocks potential re-entry attempts by S. Alam Group into four merged Shariah-compliant lenders (First Security Islamic Bank, Social Islamic Bank, Union Bank, and Global Islamic Bank) and Nassa Group's former entity Exim Bank.

The Cabinet noted that no individual or corporate entity had formally applied or met the stringent capital re-injection criteria set under Provision 18(A) prior to its repeal.

To stabilize the newly unified Sammilito Islami Bank, the government has invested Tk20,000 crore out of a total paid-up capital base of Tk35,000 crore, with the remaining Tk15,000 crore structured as depositor equity conversion.

Policy analysis

Provision 18(A) was originally drafted to minimize state-funded bailout costs by allowing former or new private investors to absorb distressed bank liabilities, cover capital deficits, and restore liquidity.

However, economic analysts, the Newspaper Owners' Association of Bangladesh (Noab), and financial watchdogs raised severe concerns regarding governance risks and moral hazard.

Economists pointed out that defaulting owners could potentially leverage loans from other domestic or offshore entities to buy back their former banks, compounding systemic vulnerability across the financial network.

Allowing groups whose management led to capital depletion to regain control undermined regulatory accountability and public trust in banking reforms.

With Tk147,000 crore in defaulted loans (representing 79% of total advance portfolios across the five merged Islamic banks), central bank intervention required public recapitalization rather than reliance on legacy shareholders.

"Repealing Provision 18(A) establishes a clear boundary between bank recovery and owner accountability," noted financial sector watchdogs.

"Allowing former controlling groups to re-acquire banks after massive capital erosion would have sent the wrong signal to depositors. Restructuring must prioritize depositor security and professional management over legacy shareholder interests."

Central bank officials clarified that revoking Provision 18(A) does not halt ongoing legal actions against defaulting groups.

"BFIU asset-tracing, account freezes, and judicial recovery processes for siphoned funds remain active independent of corporate ownership restructuring. Removing this provision simply ensures that a resolved bank remains permanently isolated from former controlling interests."

title: Energy minister: Investment-friendly policy adopted for energy sector
description:
Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood, MP, on Tuesday said the government has adopted an investment-friendly policy to increase private investment in the energy and power sectors.

He also observed that creating opportunities to earn money alone would not be enough for sustainable development of the country's industries and economy; rather, sustainable infrastructure also needs to be developed.

The minister made the remark while addressing as the chief guest a seminar titled “Crisis in the Energy Sector: Prospects and Ways Forward” organized by the Forum for Energy Reporters Bangladesh (FERB) at Dhaka Club.

State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit, MP, attended the seminar as the special guest.

Former professor of Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology and energy expert Dr Ijaz Hossain presented the keynote paper.

Iqbal Hassan Mahmood said the issue was being considered seriously so that an accident at any single LNG facility would not have a negative impact on industries across the country.

Discussions are also underway with the relevant parties on alternative arrangements and timing to address possible crises in LNG supply, he said.

He said the government remained alert to ensure that industries do not suffer, adding that discussions are underway with industrial entrepreneurs, intellectuals and experts to find ways to address the current crisis in the energy sector.

Iqbal Hasan Mahmood also referred to the meetings of the prime minister with industrial entrepreneurs within a short time after assuming office.

Cautioning against setting up coal-fired power plants, he said developed countries have reservations about coal-based power generation. Even in many cases, financing for such projects has been stopped. "So, we have to move forward very cautiously regarding these power stations," he said.

Saying that the government has taken an aggressive plan for solar power generation, the minister mentioned a new policy had been formulated within just two months. Various facilities have been kept in the policy to make it investment-friendly, including a five-year tax holiday, he added.

He said the government would implement the facilities highlighted in the policy to stop harassment of investors in the solar power sector.

The minister said: “It is our desire, and I think it is possible that we can achieve our target of 10,000 megawatts."

He said importance was being given to the OPEX model, particularly in solar power generation, and there is a plan to expand rooftop solar power gradually across the country, starting from Dhaka city.

Private investment would be encouraged instead of government investment in this regard, he said, adding that discussions had already been held with the two administrations of the Dhaka City Corporation.

He continued that an initiative is being taken to identify area-based sites and invite investors.

The minister said investors would be able to install rooftop solar power facilities, like cable television or Wi-Fi (internet) businesses, and collect bills from customers. Therefore, there is no need to depend on the government for everything, he added.

The minister also spoke of a partnership model for the use of government land in large solar power projects, under which the government could become a partner in the investment by providing land.

He said the government could provide land for the project and the value of that land could be included as the government's share within the investment structure. "I think there can be no better proposal than this," he said.

Informing about plans to further involve the private sector in importing fuel oil, the minister said unnecessary panic had been created in the country over fuel oil supplies in recent times centring on the conflict in the Middle East.

He said long queues were formed at petrol pumps in panic despite having adequate stock. Later, incidents of black-market trading and online-based fuel sales were also seen.

He said discussions had been held with the prime minister about allowing the private sector to import fuel oil following the situation.

The minister said allowing the private sector to operate alongside the government system would increase competition in the market and strengthen the supply system.

"Let there be one government [operator] and another private one, as in India," he said.

Rejecting allegations that the fuel import policy was being formulated to benefit a particular company, the minister said if it was a general law or policy, it would not be for any particular company and would apply equally to all.

"The notion that we are doing this to give it to a particular company is not correct," he said.

Urging against spreading confusion or attempts to worsen the crisis in the energy sector for political purposes, the minister said everyone would have to play a responsible role in the national interest.

He assured that investment proposals submitted by the private sector would be approved quickly if they were attractive and helpful to the industry.

Iqbal Hasan Mahmood said: "If the proposal is attractive and helpful for our industry, certainly we will not waste any time."

He further said the government would review private sector proposals seriously. After receiving a proposal, necessary approvals would be arranged following discussions and scrutiny with the concerned parties.

Bangladesh-China pledge to work together on water resources management
description:
Bangladesh and China expressed their commitment to working together on water resources management.

The two sides made the commitment as Chinese Ambassador to Bangladesh Yao Wen paid a courtesy call on Water Resources Minister Md Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee at his Secretariat office in the capital on Tuesday.

State Minister for Water Resources Forhad Hossain Azad was also present.

Anee said China and Bangladesh are long-standing and time-tested friends, and that the two countries maintain strong bilateral relations. He called for cooperation between the two countries in exchanging knowledge and experience in water resources management, education, technological cooperation, professional capacity development, and research.

Yao Wen said that China is interested in working with Bangladesh to ensure the conservation of water resources and maintain environmental balance.

He said China wants to stand by Bangladesh in addressing issues related to water resources management, floods, droughts, waterlogging, and river erosion.

Water Resources Secretary Dr AKM Shahabuddin and Chinese Embassy’s Economic and Commercial Counsellor Song Yang were present during the meeting.

title: Irene urges development partners to step up support for SDGs, LDC transition
description:
Bangladesh Permanent Representative to the United Nations (UN) in New York, Irene Khan has called upon the international community and development partners to strengthen their support for the country’s efforts to accelerate the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and ensure a sustainable graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category.

Irene Khan said this while addressing a session on the second day of the three-day national conference titled “Navigating Five Year Strategic Framework for Achieving SDGs: Policy, Partnership and Priorities”.

The parallel session titled “Role of Development Partners on Implementing Five Year Strategic Framework for Reform and Development (July 2026-June 2031) and SDGs” was held at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre (BCFCC) today, Monday, which brought together representatives of the United Nations, development partners and government officials to discuss key development priorities and partnership needs.

Irene Khan said the country was going through a rare “window of opportunity” to make a major breakthrough in its development journey.

She said the government is keen to engage with the international community to broaden and deepen discussions on development priorities and implementation of the SDGs.

Irene Khan said her role as Bangladesh’s Permanent Representative to the UN would also be to act as a bridge between the country’s development efforts and the international community, ensuring that the issues discussed at the national level receive due attention at the global level.

She noted that Bangladesh had performed well in achieving the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), but the SDGs are considerably more comprehensive, interconnected and demanding.

She stressed that the remaining period for achieving the goals would be a difficult but important journey for Bangladesh.

Referring to the government’s commitment, Khan said it is focusing on investment in key sectors, strengthening implementation and monitoring, and working closely with development partners to make up for lost time.

She also underscored the importance of domestic partners, particularly civil society and local communities, in achieving the SDGs.

“Civil society and communities have an incredibly important role to play because you’re the ones who go out there and actually are the last mile of the delivery,” she said.

She also highlighted the strong linkage between Bangladesh’s SDG implementation and its LDC graduation process.

Referring to Bangladesh’s request for a time-bound extension of the LDC graduation preparation period, Irene Khan said the extension would help the country achieve a sustainable and irreversible transition out of the LDC category.

She said the two processes create a “double incentive” for Bangladesh to accelerate reforms and development initiatives.

Irene Khan pointed out that several priorities identified in Bangladesh’s roadmap for the requested extension are closely linked to SDG implementation. These include reforms to strengthen the financial sector, improving the investment climate, enhancing domestic resource mobilisation, facilitating trade and negotiating new trade agreements.

“We would like to do, in the next three years, many of these reforms while simultaneously investing in and accelerating the delivery of the SDGs,” she said.

She urged development partners to take these two interconnected priorities into account and encourage Bangladesh on both fronts.

Describing the present period as a rare opportunity in the country’s history, Irene Khan said there is growing enthusiasm from communities to the highest levels of leadership to achieve a major development breakthrough.

She acknowledged that Bangladesh is facing difficult circumstances and resource constraints, saying the country would need to be creative and make the best possible use of its limited resources.

At the same time, she said Bangladesh has no shortage of energy, creativity and innovation and expressed confidence that these strengths can be effectively utilised to accelerate development.

Irene Khan called on the international community to stand beside Bangladesh and provide the necessary support during this critical phase of its development journey.

“We have to be creative. We have to squeeze the last penny that we have because money is short. But at the same time, there is no shortage of energy or creativity or innovation in this country,” she said.

She concluded by assuring development partners that Bangladesh would continue to engage with them at national and international levels to advance its SDG and development priorities.

Principal Coordinator on SDG Affairs at the Prime Minister’s Office SM Abdul-Awal while making his presentation sought enhanced support from development partners, including concessional financing, debt relief and technical assistance, to accelerate the country’s progress towards achieving the SDGs by 2030.

Awal said Bangladesh needs stronger partnerships and resources to implement its development priorities, particularly for marginalised and vulnerable communities.

He said Bangladesh’s performance remains weak in several SDG indicators, particularly in health, water and sanitation, affordable clean energy and other areas, while the country has made relatively better progress in poverty reduction, education and gender equality.

He identified poverty and vulnerability reduction, health and education, job creation, skills development, investment and export diversification, food security, rural enterprises, clean energy, climate resilience, and transparent and efficient service delivery as key priorities for accelerating SDG implementation by 2030.

Highlighting several flagship initiatives, including the Family Card, farmers’ initiatives, plantation programmes, e-healthcare, primary healthcare centres, education reforms, youth employment, skills development, startup funding and rural entrepreneurship, he said these programmes are aimed at improving the socioeconomic conditions of marginalised people.

“We need your support,” Abdul-Awal told development partners, seeking concessional loans, debt relief, technical assistance and increased access to development financing to support Bangladesh’s socioeconomic transformation and ensure that no one is left behind.

UN Resident Coordinator in Bangladesh Carol Flore-Smereczniak who moderated the session said development partners are ready to align their support with Bangladesh’s nationally led five-year strategic framework and help accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

She said the SDGs should not be treated as a parallel agenda, but as a practical vehicle for achieving Bangladesh’s aspirations for stronger institutions, inclusive growth, resilience and prosperity.

She said the government has set the objective of transforming Bangladesh into a trillion-dollar economy by 2034.

“Our role as development partners is to support implementation where possible and bring practical solutions that people can see and feel,” she added.

She said LDC graduation would create new opportunities but also require greater competitiveness, export diversification, stronger institutions and diversified sources of financing.

“Closing the finance gap will require a mix of domestic resource mobilisation, the quality of public spending, greater private sector participation, climate finance and continued international support,” she said.

UN Women Representative Gitanjali Singh, Valentine Achancho, country director, IFAD, Diepak Elmer, the Charge d’ Affaires and head of cooperation at the Embassy of Switzerland, Adam Aspden, British high commission, Edwin Koekkoek, first counsellor, acting head of Cooperation, EU, Sonali Dayaratne, deputy resident representative, UNDP, Felix Helgesson, deputy head of development Cooperation, Embassy of Sweden, Hasina Begum, social policy manager, UNICEF, Farzana Dorin, national professional officer, Policies for Prevention of NCDs, WHO, Dhruv Sharma, senior economist, World Bank, Owais Parray, senior economist, UNDP, and Sardar Asaduzzaman, assistant resident representative, UNDP, spoke among others at the session.

title: High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi conveyed Dhaka's message to Modi in Delhi
description:
Indian High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi conveyed Dhaka's message to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi regarding the creation of a 'supportive environment' to advance the relationship with Bangladesh.

Following a series of meetings with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and other top government officials, Dinesh Trivedi met with Narendra Modi in Delhi on Tuesday.

According to diplomatic sources from both countries, several sensitive issues affecting the relationship between the two nations also came up during the discussions.

A diplomatic source from Delhi told Prothom Alo that High Commissioner Dinesh Trivedi called on Prime Minister Narendra Modi today, Tuesday and sought his guidance on further strengthening the multifaceted and enduring bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh in a constructive manner with a people-centric approach.

Multiple diplomatic sources from India informed this correspondent that Dinesh Trivedi met Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the Parliament building around 6 PM local time on Tuesday, and their discussion lasted about an hour.

Diplomatic sources hinted that the message from Bangladesh, which was conveyed during the recent meetings with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman, and Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed in Dhaka, was presented to Prime Minister Modi by the Indian High Commissioner in Delhi.

According to official sources in Dhaka, during an initial courtesy call with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Monday, the topic of the Delhi visit was also brought up by the Indian High Commissioner.

He mentioned that the Government of India is keen to welcome Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his family for a visit to Delhi.

Commenting on the meeting with the Prime Minister during a briefing at the Foreign Ministry, Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman emphasised the importance placed by Bangladesh on creating the ''enabling environment'' necessary for advancing bilateral relations.

In his words, "It's crucial to establish the environment needed to move the relationship forward."

After separate meetings with the Prime Minister, Foreign Minister, and Home Minister on Monday, the Indian High Commissioner spoke to journalists at the Home Ministry.

He stated that maintaining a good relationship with Bangladesh is ''especially important, '' a point repeatedly emphasised by India's Prime Minister.

Joblessness, skills gap, digital addiction challenge Bangladesh’s youth
description:
“Degrees, but no jobs”; “skills, but no opportunities”; “dreams, but no proper guidance”—these concerns reflect the reality faced by many young people in Bangladesh, according to a nationwide youth survey.

Unemployment, skills gaps, mental stress, digital addiction, online gambling and drug abuse, along with limited youth participation in policymaking, have emerged as major concerns among the country’s young people.

The survey, titled “Problems of Youth in Bangladesh and Possible Solutions,” was jointly conducted by Shopnopuri Kallyan Sangstha and Bangladesh Co-Creation to mark International Youth Day 2026.

Students, youth organizers, volunteers, social and development workers, and representatives of youth initiatives from different parts of the country participated in the survey.

An analysis of the responses shows a common reality: young people have considerable potential but lack adequate opportunities, skills, guidance and platforms to realize it.

Unemployment remains a major concern

Many respondents identified unemployment as one of the biggest challenges facing young people.

Abu Huraira Sheikh, a member of FFCRJ, and Md Mahibullah, general secretary of Nobojagoron Chhatra Sangha, said many young people struggle to find suitable employment even after completing their education.

They said the problem is not simply a shortage of jobs but also a significant mismatch between labor market demands and the skills and preparation of young jobseekers.

As a result, many educated young people remain unemployed or underemployed for extended periods.

Degrees without adequate skills

Many respondents said Bangladesh’s education system remains largely examination- and certificate-oriented.

Kaunik Debnath, director of programs and operations at Ancora, said many young people hold multiple academic certificates but lack adequate communication skills, technological knowledge, problem-solving abilities and workplace presentation skills.

Tanjela Akter Ema, volunteer coordinator at Bengal Peace Foundation, identified the lack of practical experience and career guidance as major challenges.

Nandita Rani Pal, a student at Daffodil International University; Md Zubayer Ahmed, president of Udarata Youth Foundation; and Ahmad Saeed, founder of Changemakers United, expressed similar concerns.

They said digital skills, English proficiency, information technology, artificial intelligence and practical work experience are becoming increasingly important in the labor market alongside academic qualifications.

Gap between education and employment

Sadia Tabassum, a student at Begum Badrunnesa Government Girls’ College, said many students spend years pursuing education without gaining sufficient understanding of workplace realities.

Md Abdullah Al Mamun Khan, chief executive officer of IVDS Foundation, and Dhruva Chowdhury, a volunteer at OAB Foundation, stressed the need for more hands-on learning, internships, apprenticeships and job-oriented training.

They also called for stronger links between educational institutions and industries so students can gain practical experience alongside their studies.

Mental stress: A silent crisis

The survey also highlighted growing concerns about the mental well-being of young people.

Saleha K, a member of Disable Welfare Society Bangladesh, identified rising frustration and depression among young people as major concerns.

Rabiul Islam, organizing secretary of Gabura Welfare Society, said uncertainty about the future, lack of confidence and inadequate guidance are making many young people increasingly vulnerable to mental stress.

Sanjida Sumiya Suchona, a representative of Geo Avengers, said many young people are becoming frustrated because even after years of education and skills development, they cannot be assured of desired jobs, financial stability or a better quality of life.

She also identified global economic uncertainty, inflation, the climate crisis, political instability and wars as additional sources of pressure.

Digital addiction, online gambling raise concern

Respondents also expressed concern about excessive use of digital technology, online gambling and casino games.

Md Shariful Islam Abhi, founder and director of Islamic Society Sangha Burimari, highlighted mobile phone misuse and drug addiction among young people.

Ayesha Khatun Asha, community facilitator at Youth for Change, said excessive mobile phone use is contributing to reduced attention, wasted time and growing social isolation.

Md Golam Momin, a student at Jatiya Kabi Kazi Nazrul Islam University, identified online gambling and betting as growing threats.

He said the lure of making quick money is pushing many young people toward risky activities.

Reading and social engagement declining

Md Riaz-ul Islam, a volunteer at OAB Foundation, highlighted declining interest in reading among young people.

He said reading is important not only for increasing knowledge but also for developing critical thinking, creativity and values.

Several respondents also said young people’s participation in social and volunteer activities is declining.

Such activities, they noted, can help develop leadership, teamwork and a sense of social responsibility.

Lack of direction and fear of failure

Iti, a program officer at Ancora, said many young people struggle to make decisions based on their potential and abilities because they lack clear goals.

Adel Hossain, general secretary of Independent Blood Bank, said many young people hesitate to start something new because they fear failure. Some also lose interest soon after starting, he added.

He stressed the importance of patience and consistency in developing skills and achieving success.

Youth participation in decision-making remains limited

Jaki Mujahidul Islam, founder and executive director of Fridays for Rights, identified the lack of youth empowerment as a fundamental challenge.

Saifullah Bin Rafiq Chowdhury, finance coordinator at Rise Up, said that although various plans and programs are developed for young people, their participation in policymaking and decision-making remains limited.

As a result, many initiatives do not fully reflect the actual needs of young people, he said.

Migration and a ‘transit mindset’

A relatively different concern was raised by Aman Ullah, adviser to Dipanchal Foundation.

He said a “transit mindset” is emerging among many young people, with many viewing Bangladesh as a temporary stop rather than a place where they envision their long-term future.

Increasingly, he said, young people view migration abroad as the primary pathway to success.

This could reduce their long-term engagement in solving local problems, developing communities and pursuing social initiatives.

To address the issue, Aman Ullah proposed a “Local Stake Initiative” to make young people partners in local development projects.

Young people also point to solutions

Survey respondents proposed a range of solutions, including skills-based education, technical and digital training, internships, career counseling, mentorship, entrepreneurship development, accessible financing, mental health support and greater social engagement.

They said an environment needs to be created where education, skills, employment, mental well-being and civic participation complement one another.

Young people, they said, should not be viewed merely as beneficiaries of development but also as partners in driving it.

title: Bangladesh, Singapore discuss skills dev, migrant worker welfare, investment
description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam on Tuesday said Bangladesh is placing strong emphasis on developing skilled manpower, with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman giving special attention to technical and vocational education and training (TVET).

She made the remarks during a meeting with Dinesh Vasu Dash, Singapore’s minister of State for Manpower and minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth.

Shama Obaed said Singapore, as a pioneer in skills development and capacity building, could support Bangladesh in these areas and proposed greater cooperation between the relevant agencies of the two countries, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

During the meeting, she highlighted the strong and long-standing relations between Bangladesh and Singapore.

The state minister said the government of Bangladesh is committed to fairness, good governance and creating better opportunities for its people.

She also highlighted the important role of the large Bangladeshi community in Singapore.

Dinesh Vasu agreed that both countries share common interests in promoting skilled manpower.

He suggested that the relevant government agencies of Bangladesh and Singapore could establish closer contact and work together.

The Singaporean state minister also appreciated the contribution of Bangladeshi migrant workers to Singapore and mentioned that they are generally disciplined and responsible.

In response, Shama Obaed said Bangladesh is also focusing on language proficiency for Bangladeshi expatriates and encouraging them to learn a third language.

She informed that women constitute around half of Bangladesh’s population and have significant potential to work in the care and nursing sectors.

The state minister proposed that Singapore could consider providing relevant training for Bangladeshi nurses who could come to Singapore as caregivers for elderly people.

She also proposed cooperation between major public hospitals in Bangladesh and Singapore, including Dhaka Medical College Hospital, Singapore General Hospital and National University Hospital, in areas of mutual interest.

The two sides also discussed the recruitment of migrant workers.

Dinesh Vasu expressed concern about the costs and fees involved in the recruitment process.

In response, Shama Obaed said the government of Bangladesh is determined to reduce recruitment costs and regulate and streamline recruiting agencies.

She proposed that Bangladesh and Singapore could explore ways to jointly monitor recruitment practices, including the role of intermediaries and travel agencies, to make the recruitment process more transparent, accountable and affordable.

Dinesh Vasu briefed Shama Obaed on Singapore’s initiatives to improve migrant workers’ accommodation.

He said the government of Singapore has introduced major initiatives to upgrade migrant worker dormitories and enforce stricter housing standards.

The Singaporean state minister added that their government continues to balance the demand for migrant workers with the availability of suitable accommodation.

The Bangladesh state minister appreciated these initiatives and expressed gratitude to the government of Singapore for its prompt action to arrange re-employment and compensation for around 200 Bangladeshi workers who recently lost their jobs following the bankruptcy of three companies in Singapore.

Dinesh Vasu encouraged migrant workers to report cases of unpaid wages to the Ministry of Manpower so that the authorities can take appropriate action and provide the necessary assistance and compensation.

He also appreciated the positive role of Bangladeshi workers in Singapore’s community programs and celebrations, noting that their participation contributes to racial and social harmony in Singapore.

Shama Obaed invited Dinesh Vasu to visit Bangladesh. She said there are many opportunities for cooperation between the two countries in engaging young people and building their skills.

She also suggested that a Singaporean team from the relevant agencies could visit Bangladesh to explore possible areas of cooperation.

Nodding positively to this proposal, Dinesh Vasu, in view of his additional portfolio as minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth, expressed interest in exploring opportunities for further cooperation in these areas.

The Bangladesh state minister also sought Singapore’s support for Bangladesh’s aspiration to become a Dialogue Partner of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).

She said Bangladesh is giving greater importance to soft diplomacy, particularly cultural and sports diplomacy.

Shama Obaed informed that the government of Bangladesh has allocated a budget for the creative economy in the current fiscal year.

She also proposed establishing a youth centre in either Dhaka or Singapore to facilitate the exchange of innovative ideas and promote cooperation among young people.

The state minister further highlighted Bangladesh’s focus on joint ventures, investment and entrepreneurship.

She said Bangladesh is working to create a more investment-friendly environment and provide a hassle-free business environment through measures such as one-stop services. She also highlighted the importance of ensuring a secure and safe environment for investors.

In this connection, Dinesh Vasu mentioned the presence of Singaporean businesses in Bangladesh, referring to the Singapore-based restaurant chain named “Fish & Co”, which recently opened in Dhaka.

Shama Obaed also highlighted the importance of cultural and economic diplomacy and greater people-to-people engagement between Bangladesh and Singapore.

She said Bangladesh is keen to expand cooperation in these areas and create new opportunities for both countries.

Both sides expressed their readiness to further strengthen bilateral cooperation, particularly in the areas of skilled manpower, vocational training, migrant worker welfare, youth development, investment, culture and people-to-people connectivity.
